messages.subject: Variable transect lengths
parts:
Hello,
I'm new to Distance, and have been trying to teach myself with the books. I may have missed it, but could you please tell me what is the best way to deal with variable transect lengths? 
I'm dealing with marine mammal data collected on ferries (I realise this isn't an ideal survey design), where effort ends as rough weather or darkness approaches. As a result, I have many transects of different lengths. I've read a few studies that split the transect into segments of equal length - is this the best way to proceed?
Best,
James

messages.subject: Re: Variable transect lengths
parts:
Hi James,

I am dealing with data from a similar set up (collected via cruise ships) ad was kindly directed to a few resources and given some important bits of advice. I'll link to/paste the responses I got below for your reference as well.

Hope these are helpful to you,
Sara



From Eric Rexstad:
https://groups.google.com/d/msg/distance-sampling/ZakrkcgpMs4/nvamOCGPEQAJ

From Rob Williams:
There isn’t a transect per se in a platform of opportunity study. Instead, you divide your effort into roughly evenly sized segments. Then, you can specify the size of a moving block (# of segments) to use in DSM in Distance to estimate variance. If you are doing this in R, you have more options for estimating variance. If you like, you can try setting each trip as a resampling unit with a bootstrap or jackknife. We tried that with Antarctic cruise ships: 

http://www.ecologyandsociety.org/vol11/iss1/art1/

The newer variance propagation methods based on segments are now integrated into Distance, and they don’t require you to specify a resampling unit. They do require a bunch of work to divide your tracks into segments that are short enough to have environmental conditions remain more or less constant along the segment, and long enough so that you don’t have a major problem with over dispersion. You wouldn’t want 100,000, 1km segments that had 99,950 zeroes and 50 ones.   
http://www.nature.com/articles/srep04170
https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Alexandre_Zerbini/publication/50347370_Chilean_Blue_Whales_as_a_Case_Study_to_Illustrate_Methods_to_Estimate_Abundance_and_Evaluate_Conservation_Status_of_Rare_Species/links/09e4150f4f39f662a4000000.pdf

The best primer for this is David Miller’s recent review of DSM: http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12105/abstract  No doubt you’ve read this already.
